opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind the responsible scaling policy is that we shouldn't be setting safety measures based on where models are today. We should tie them to what the models can actually do. As capabilities increase, the required precautions increase with them.

The way we've structured it is around AI Safety Levels, or ASLs, loosely modeled on the biosafety level system for handling dangerous pathogens. Each level comes with two kinds of commitments. One is containment: how well are we securing the model weights, so that someone can't steal them and strip off the safeguards? The other is deployment: what protections do we put in place so that people using the model can't misuse it for something catastrophic, like meaningful uplift toward bioweapons?

The thing I find most compelling is that it turns a vague debate into something more concrete. Instead of arguing in the abstract about whether AI is dangerous, you say: here are specific capabilities we're worried about. Here are evaluations that test for them. If a model crosses a threshold, we either have the corresponding safeguards ready or we don't train further or deploy until we do. That creates a real incentive internally. If the safety work isn't done, it blocks the product, so safety research becomes something the whole company needs to get right, not a side project.

That said, I think there are some genuinely hard parts. One is that evaluations are difficult. You're trying to rule out a capability, and it's easy to under-elicit what a model can do. Someone with more time, better prompting, or fine-tuning might get much more out of it than your evals did. So you need buffers and you need to keep improving the evals themselves.

Another is that the higher levels get really demanding. Defending model weights against a well-resourced state actor is an extremely hard security problem. And for the most capable systems, we're going to need things we don't fully know how to do yet, like better interpretability or other ways of getting real assurance that a model isn't pursuing goals we didn't intend. Part of the point of the policy is to be honest that we have to solve those problems before we get there, not after.

And finally, I don't think any single company's policy is sufficient. Ideally these commitments become a template that other labs adopt and eventually inform regulation, so there's a shared floor rather than a race where whoever is least careful sets the pace. So my view is: tie safeguards to capabilities, measure carefully, be willing to actually pause if you're not ready, and keep iterating on the policy as we learn more, because we definitely won't get it perfect the first time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions catastrophic misuse and bioweapons, but does not identify nonexperts creating mass-casualty weapons as easily as experts as a threshold.

r002.rationale: It says that if a model crosses a capability threshold, safeguards must be ready or training and deployment pause.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluations for specific capabilities, but does not say they should warn before the model reaches the dangerous capability.

r004.rationale: It does not state that crossing an early-warning evaluation threshold should trigger reassessment.

r005.rationale: It calls for iterating on the policy but does not describe defining the subsequent risk level when the next level is reached.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the core of the RSP is this idea of AI safety levels, which we borrowed loosely from the biosafety levels that labs use for handling dangerous pathogens. The basic structure is: you define thresholds of capability that would be dangerous, you define the safety and security measures that need to be in place before you train or deploy a model at that level, and you commit ahead of time to not crossing a threshold until those measures are ready.

I think the key thing — and the thing I find most compelling about the approach — is that the commitments are made in advance, before you're under pressure. If you wait until you have a model that's clearly very capable and very commercially valuable, and then try to decide whether it's safe to deploy, you're going to be making that decision in the worst possible environment. There's a lot of incentive to rationalise. So the idea is to figure out now, while things are calmer, what capabilities we'd be worried about, how we'd test for them, and what we'd need to have in place.

Concretely, that means things like: for each safety level you specify evaluations that act as tripwires. If a model shows meaningful uplift on, say, bioweapons-relevant tasks, or shows signs of being able to autonomously replicate or do substantial AI R&D on its own, that triggers a requirement for a higher level of protection — stronger security against model weights being stolen, better deployment safeguards, possibly things we haven't fully worked out yet. And if you can't meet the requirements, the honest answer is you pause. You don't train or deploy the next model until you can.

I'll be upfront that there are a lot of hard parts. One is that evaluations are genuinely difficult — you have to run them often enough that you don't blow past a threshold without noticing, and you have to worry about underestimating a model's capabilities because you didn't elicit them well. We try to build in buffers for that. Another is that for the higher levels, we don't yet know exactly what safety measures would be sufficient, and I think it's important to be honest about that rather than pretend we have it figured out. The policy is explicitly meant to be iterated on as we learn more.

The other thing I'd say is that I don't think a voluntary policy from one company is the end state. What I hope is that it's a useful template — that it demonstrates one concrete way of doing this, that other labs adopt something similar, and that eventually something like it gets encoded in regulation so it's not just relying on companies choosing to hold themselves to it. But in the meantime, I think having a public, specific commitment that people can hold us accountable to is a lot better than nothing.

r001.rationale: The response mentions bioweapons-relevant tasks, but does not identify nonexperts creating mass-casualty weapons as easily as experts as a dangerous threshold.

r002.rationale: It says safety and security measures must be ready before training or deploying a model at a designated capability level, and says to pause if requirements are unmet.

r003.rationale: It describes evaluations as tripwires, but does not clearly state that they should signal danger before the model reaches the dangerous capability itself.

r004.rationale: It says an evaluation result triggers stronger protection, but does not clearly say crossing an early-warning threshold should trigger reassessment.

r005.rationale: It discusses multiple safety levels and iterating the policy, but does not describe defining the subsequent risk level when the next level is reached.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make the policy a concrete commitment: as models become more capable of causing harm, the safeguards we require should become stronger. And if we can’t establish that those safeguards are adequate, we shouldn’t keep scaling or deploying the model until they are.

That requires defining thresholds ahead of time. What capabilities would make a model substantially more dangerous? What evaluations would tell us we’re approaching that point? And what security and deployment protections would we need before crossing it? You want those decisions made before there’s a lot of pressure to release a particular model.

There’s also a difficult uncertainty problem. A model failing to demonstrate a dangerous capability in an evaluation doesn’t necessarily mean it lacks that capability. So the policy needs a margin of safety, and the evaluations need to improve as the models improve.

Ultimately, I’d judge the policy by whether it changes what we do. Does it lead us to invest in safeguards earlier? Would it actually cause us to pause when we couldn’t meet the requirements? That’s what makes it meaningful.

r002.rationale: It says safeguards should be adequate before scaling or deployment, but does not state that mitigations must be in place before training models with designated red-line capabilities.

r003.rationale: It asks which evaluations would show that a model is approaching the dangerous capability threshold, communicating an early warning before the model reaches it.

r004.rationale: It says the policy should cause a pause if requirements cannot be met, but does not say that crossing an early-warning evaluation threshold should trigger reassessment.

r005.rationale: It calls for defining thresholds and protections in advance, but does not describe defining a subsequent risk level when the next level is reached.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make commitments before you’re under pressure to deploy a particular model. You want to specify what capabilities would make a model substantially more dangerous, how you’ll test for those capabilities, and what safeguards you’d need before training or deploying a system that crosses those thresholds.

Those are two different kinds of safeguards. One is security: can you prevent someone from stealing the model weights and removing the protections? The other is deployment safety: can you prevent people from using the model to cause serious harm through the product? You need both.

And the policy has to have teeth. If a model reaches a dangerous capability threshold and the required safeguards aren’t ready, the response has to be to pause the relevant development or deployment until they are. Otherwise, you’ve described an aspiration rather than a constraint.

There’s also a lot of uncertainty about how to measure these capabilities. So I’d want the policy to improve as we learn, with external scrutiny and enough transparency that people can assess whether the commitments are actually being met. The important thing is that uncertainty shouldn’t automatically become a reason to keep going.
